title: Identification of possible risc factors concerning the outcome of metastatic lung cancer patients on the intensive care unit
summary:
Lung cancer is one of the most frequently diagnosed malignancies and, globally, the leading cause of cancer-related deaths. Despite advances in treatment, the long-term overall survival rate remains poor, particularly among patients with metastatic tumors.
Over the past decade, improvements in prognosis for these patients have been reported worldwide. However, lung cancer continues to be associated with a significantly poorer prognosis in the intensive care unit (ICU) compared to other solid tumors. It remains unclear which subset of lung cancer patients benefits from intensive care treatment—particularly when ventilatory support is required.
The objective of this monocentric retrospective study is to identify parameters and factors that may be associated with the prognosis and clinical course of lung cancer patients in the ICU.
The following parameters will be documented: age, sex, date of ICU admission, reason for intubation (if applicable), duration of ventilation, ventilation pressures, and patient weaning status. Additionally, pre-existing conditions—such as COPD, coronary artery disease (CAD), history of smoking, or severe obesity—will be recorded. Microbiological findings will also be documented. The collected parameters will be correlated with prognostic and clinical outcome measures, such as the duration of hospital stay and the duration of invasive ventilation.
The aim of this study is to identify prognostically significant factors associated with the prognosis and clinical course of these patients in the ICU, thereby helping to answer the question of which lung cancer patients truly benefit from intensive care treatment.
